title: Where U.S. K-12 stands
lede: Five school years after the pandemic closures, achievement is still below 2019 in every NAEP grade and subject, the lowest-performing students are falling furthest behind, and attendance recovery has nearly stalled. Enrollment is shrinking, teacher pay is rising in nominal terms, and federal governance is being reorganized in real time.

kpis.label: Grade 8 math, NAEP average
kpis.note: Flat vs 2022. Students at the 10th percentile fell 5 more points while the 90th percentile rose 3.

kpis.label: Chronically absent students
kpis.note: Down less than 1 point in a year after drops of nearly 3 and just over 2 points; about 29% of students are in districts on pace to halve 2022 rates by 2027.

kpis.label: Public school enrollment
kpis.note: Down 1.4 million from the 2019 peak of 50.8M. NCES projects fewer than 47M by 2030.

kpis.label: Average teacher salary
kpis.note: Starting salary $48,112 (+3.4%); after inflation, starting pay grew just 0.7%.

kpis.label: Teaching positions unfilled or not fully certified
kpis.note: 387,843 teachers not fully certified for their assignment (50 states + DC) plus 37,569 vacancies (29 states + DC).

kpis.label: Current spending per pupil
kpis.note: Record high in nominal terms. New York spends most ($31,918); Idaho least ($11,060).

chart.title: NAEP average scores, 2013–2024
chart.subtitle: The 'learning recession' predates the pandemic: scores peaked around 2013 and every grade and subject is now below 2019. Panels share one vertical scale (same points per pixel) around each grade's own level.
chart.note: Rounded national averages from the NAEP Data Service; NCES computes reported differences from unrounded scores (for example, grade 4 math is reported as +2 vs 2022 and −3 vs 2019).

items.headline: No subject or grade is back to 2019.
items.detail: Only two states beat their own pre-pandemic score anywhere: Louisiana (grade 4 reading) and Alabama (grade 4 math).

items.headline: Reading fell again in both grades.
items.detail: 33% of 8th graders read below NAEP Basic, the largest share ever; about 40% of 4th graders are below Basic, the most since 2002.

items.headline: The gap between top and bottom is widening.
items.detail: The lowest performers score about 100 points below the highest; gaps have grown for roughly a decade.

items.headline: Seniors hit record lows.
items.detail: Grade 12 math and reading each fell 3 points from 2019; 45% of seniors are below Basic in math and 33% are academically prepared for college math (37% in 2019).

chart.title: Chronic absenteeism, 2018–2025
chart.subtitle: Share of K-12 public school students missing 10% or more of the school year (45 states with 2025 data).
chart.note: 2020 and 2021 omitted: remote instruction made attendance data unreliable. School years are labeled by their spring.

items.label: Students in districts on pace to halve 2022 absenteeism by 2027
items.note: 18 states have formally adopted the halve-by-2027 target.

items.label: States with rates of 30% or higher
items.note: Alaska, District of Columbia, Oregon, New Mexico.

items.label: First states reporting 2025–26 rates
items.note: CO, CT, GA, LA, MA, RI; Rhode Island is within half a point of its pre-pandemic baseline.

items.label: Learning lost to elevated absenteeism
items.note: Recovery would have been 0.03–0.05 grade levels larger had attendance returned to 2019 levels.

chart.title: Public school enrollment, fall 2019–2024
chart.subtitle: Millions of PK-12 students in public schools; the axis starts at 46 million, not zero. Falling births, more homeschooling and private choice, and migration all contribute.
chart.note: NCES counts; FutureEd analysis updated July 2026. Kindergarten alone lost 237,000 students (−6%) between 2019 and 2024 while high school grew 2%.

items.label: Schools slated to close in 2026 across 14 districts
items.note: Enrollment fell in 40 states between 2019 and 2024; 16 states lost 5% or more.

items.label: Homeschool enrollment growth, 2024–25
items.note: Ten reporting states hit record homeschool counts.

items.label: Students in private school choice programs
items.note: 75 programs in 34 states, DC and Puerto Rico; about 2.8% of all students.

items.label: States opted into the federal scholarship tax credit
items.note: Dollar-for-dollar credit up to $1,700 for donations to scholarship organizations, starting Jan 1, 2027.

chart.title: Average teacher salary, highest and lowest states
chart.subtitle: 2024–25, not adjusted for cost of living. National average: $74,495.

items.label: Teachers reporting frequent job-related stress
items.note: Down from 62% in 2025, but still far above comparable adults on every well-being indicator.

items.label: Teachers intending to leave the profession
items.note: About one in four plan to stay as long as they are able; 30% hold a job outside their school system.

items.label: States reporting math teacher shortages
items.note: Math, special education and science are the three most common shortage areas; 48 states report at least one.

items.label: States where the average starting salary tops $50,000
items.note: National average starting salary: $48,112. U.S. public schools employed 3,231,992 teachers in 2024–25, about 15.1 students per teacher.

items.headline: FY 2026 federal funding held steady.
items.detail: The deal signed February 3, 2026 gives the Education Department $79B in discretionary funds; Title I and IDEA each gained $20M, and a provision bars transferring ED funds to other agencies unless Congress specifies it.

items.headline: The Department keeps handing off programs.
items.detail: Fourteen interagency agreements with six agencies were announced between May 2025 and June 16, 2026, moving Title I administration, special education, CTE and civil rights work to Labor, HHS, Justice and others. Several are being challenged in court.

items.headline: Per-pupil spending hit a record.
items.detail: Current spending rose 6.6% to $17,619 in FY 2024, the last year with pandemic relief. Instruction was 58.8% of current spending.

items.headline: Universal choice is now the norm in a fifth of states.
items.detail: Roughly 18 states offer universal or near-universal private-choice eligibility; Arizona's ESA program alone tops 99,000 students. Half the states have already opted into the 2027 federal tax-credit scholarship.

items.label: Cellphone laws
items.note: Enacted legislation on student phone use, from bell-to-bell bans to guidance and pouch funding (NCSL, July 2026).

items.label: Science of reading
items.note: Laws or policies requiring evidence-based reading instruction since 2013 (EdWeek, Aug 2026).

items.label: Math instruction laws
items.note: Since 2022; nine states acted in 2026 alone (EdWeek, Aug 2026).

items.label: K-12 AI guidance
items.note: Official state guidance or policy on AI in schools (AI for Education, Aug 21, 2026).

items.label: Companion chatbot laws
items.note: Laws regulating AI companion chatbots enacted in 2026, most with minor-specific protections and most effective in 2027 (MultiState).

items.headline: One school in three has recovered in a subject; one in seven in both.
items.detail: NWEA's study of 5 million students in 9,326 schools defines recovery as fall 2024 achievement at or above fall 2019. High-poverty schools are less likely to be recovered but have made the largest gains.

items.headline: The recovery is U-shaped by income.
items.detail: The highest- and lowest-income districts improved most from 2022 to 2025; middle-income districts (30–70% subsidized lunch) improved least, largely because federal relief was concentrated at the extremes.

items.headline: Reading shows its first turnaround.
items.detail: Math rebounded immediately after 2022 while reading kept falling through 2024; 2025 brought the first reading gains, all in states implementing comprehensive science-of-reading reforms (DC, IN, KY, MD, MN, MS, LA, TN).

items.headline: 108 'districts on the rise' outpace their peers.
items.detail: Districts that gained at least 0.3 grade levels in both subjects relative to matched peers in their own state, showing demographics are not destiny.

items.label: Americans giving their community's schools an A or B

delta.text: lowest since 2004; 13% for the nation's schools

items.note: 86% support some form of school cellphone ban; 64% say teacher pay is too low; 66% oppose closing the Education Department.

items.label: Americans satisfied with K-12 education quality
items.note: Parents rate their own child's school far higher: 74% satisfied.

items.label: High schoolers with persistent sadness or hopelessness
items.note: 20.4% seriously considered suicide; 53% of girls reported persistent sadness. 2025 YRBS results are pending.

items.label: Four-year high school graduation rate
items.note: Adjusted cohort graduation rate; up from 80% in 2011–12. Class of 2025 averages: SAT 1029, ACT 19.4.
